name: The imaginative background of physics: Will as the source of motion
plain_explanation: Every philosopher, beneath their formal theory, has a simpler picture of how the world 'basically' works; for Aristotle and most Greeks, since the two most obviously self-moving things were animals and the heavenly bodies, the natural assumption was that all motion ultimately traces back to some kind of Will -- the capricious will of animals and humans on earth, the perfect, orderly will of a Divine Being in the heavens.
precise_definition: Russell's own interpretive thesis (borrowing Santayana's phrase 'animal faith') that beneath Aristotle's explicit physical doctrines lies an unstated, pre-theoretical picture in which motion is modeled on animal self-movement and the willed regularity of divinized heavenly bodies, rather than on the strictly mechanical picture of later physics.
why_it_mattered: It explains, for Russell, why Aristotle's physics assimilates inanimate motion to purposive, quasi-biological behavior, and why this made his physics an obstacle rather than an aid to the eventual mechanical, mathematical physics of Galileo and Newton.
historical_origin: Russell's own diagnostic framework, applied to Aristotle but stated as a general claim about all philosophers' unstated 'crude' systems.
examples: A modern child distinguishes live animals from other things by their capacity for self-movement; Russell suggests this same childhood intuition, generalized by Aristotle into an adult theory, became the basis of his physics.
Anaxagoras was prosecuted for impiety for denying the sun and moon were alive -- showing how deeply the divinity of heavenly bodies was assumed in Greek culture.
competing_positions: The modern, mechanical imaginative background (motor-cars, aeroplanes, machines) in which 'animals have lost their importance' as models for lifeless motion.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Rooted in the widespread Greek religious assumption, instilled in childhood, that the sun and moon are gods.
